title: U.S. Tennis Association hires Craig Tiley as chief executive from Australian Open
content:
Craig Tiley is the new chief executive of the U.S. Tennis Association.

Tiley, the former Australian Open tournament director and Tennis Australia chief executive who has developed a reputation as one of the more forward-thinking people in the sport, has joined on a longterm contract.

He will not be tournament director for the U.S. Open, instead working alongside Eric Butorac, an architect of the tournament’s $1-million, star-spangled mixed doubles tournament who replaced Stacey Allaster in the role last fall. Tiley replaces Lew Sherr, who last summer left the USTA to join the New York Mets as chief executive.

“From the very beginning of this process, our top priority was identifying the right leader to accelerate participation growth and help us achieve our goal of reaching 35 million players by 2035,” said USTA Board Chair and interim co-chief executive Brian Vahaly.

“Craig brings a rare combination of global credibility at the highest level of the sport and a proven commitment to growing the game at the grassroots. That balance is exactly what this moment requires. As we look to fully leverage the power of the U.S. Open as a platform for inspiration and growth, Craig’s leadership and understanding of the entire tennis ecosystem will be invaluable.

“We are excited to build on our current momentum of six consecutive years of participation growth, and we are confident he is the right leader to guide American tennis into its next chapter.”

In a statement that accompanied the announcement, Tiley said, “I am truly honored to step into the role of CEO of the USTA later this year. I’ve long admired the organization’s leadership in growing the game across the United States and the extraordinary success of the US Open.

“Tennis has shaped my life — personally and professionally — and having begun my tennis journey in the U.S. as an NCAA championship coach, this opportunity feels like a full-circle moment. I’m excited to return to American tennis and to work alongside our leadership locally and nationally to continue building the sport’s reach, impact, and future.”

Tiley’s final act as Australian Open tournament director was to posit another string of possible innovations at the tournament, including women playing best-of-five-set matches from the quarterfinals onward, something at which WTA stars have largely balked. Tiley also proposed remaking the look of the tennis court, beginning with getting rid of the umpire’s chair. Umpires would still have a role in overseeing matches, but they would carry that out from a bunker underneath the stadium.

From there, they could come onto the court to settle any disputes that arise.

Tiley also wants to get rid of the warmup time ahead of the match, end “lets” on serve, and change player benches will convert to mini performance centers, with data screens and heating and cooling technology. For fans, he proposed more space, shade, seats and screens, at a tournament whose popularity, attendance figures and revenues have risen to record highs under his purview.

While Tiley and the Australian Open have long set the pace for innovation in the sport, there was a sense that he could only have so much impact far from the sport’s power centers in Europe and the U.S.. That became evident in 2024, when Tiley, largely in concert with Sherr and other organizers, tried to lead an effort from the Grand Slams to create a streamlined schedule — a so-called premium tour.

Various similar versions of that plan have been passed around meeting tables by the governing bodies, and some version of it will likely emerge from the inertia-slowed reckoning that tennis is currently undergoing about its future.

At the USTA, Tiley will have the power and influence that usually comes with a larger purse. USTA revenues have climbed to roughly $650 million per year. Australia collects a little more than $400 million.

The USTA will provide Tiley with a more impactful canvas to pursue further innovation, led by a tournament that has long marketed itself as a celebration of New York’s food, fashion and celebrity culture, with a bit of tennis mixed in.

A rotating cast of disc jockeys spins music during changeovers; scoreboards show off the work of the tournament’s “spotters,” who tip off camera people as to where the glitterati are sitting during matches.

That said, Tiley basically ran his own show in Australia. The U.S. is more than 10 times larger by population. The USTA board, with its representation from all the different tennis regions, can be unwieldy.

He joins the USTA with more changes to steward. Before Sherr left the organization, he announced an $800 million renovation of Arthur Ashe Stadium, the 24,000-capacity main arena at the U.S. Open and the biggest stadium in the sport. It will consist of a $250 million player performance center and changes to seating structure, adding more seats in more expensive ticketing tiers.

Tiley’s changes at his former employer and those he will oversee at his new one are part of the endless Grand Slam arms race, in which the Australian Open and U.S. Open are the lead runners. Both have successfully converted two-week tennis tournaments into three-week festivals, with the U.S. Open the first to stage a fully fledged event (the mixed doubles) in the so-called Week 0, previously reserved for qualifying and fan events.

The Australian Open responded this year by expanding its “Opening Week” program with the “One Point Slam,” a mixed pro-am competition which filled Rod Laver Arena and generated buzz and goodwill among top stars without overtaxing them on the court. The U.S. Open calls its version of that week “Fan Week.”

The French Open holds qualifying matches on some of its biggest courts the week before its main draw, with Wimbledon lagging behind its three competitors as it bids to move qualifying on-site through an expansion currently held up by legal challenges.

Legal challenges also define Tiley’s other key responsibility as he joins the USTA. Under Tiley’s stewardship, Tennis Australia broke with the other three Grand Slam organizers by agreeing a settlement with a player association over an antitrust lawsuit against the four majors and men’s and women’s tours.

Tennis Australia agreed to provide the Professional Tennis Players’ Association (PTPA) with access to internal documents and other filings in discovery, essentially switching sides from defendant to collaborator and angering the other three majors sufficiently that they all considered not attending the 2026 Australian Open.

Tiley is a native of South Africa, but his journey in tennis involves deep ties to the U.S.. He coached the men’s team at the University of Illinois from 1994 to 2005, winning the NCAA title in 2003 with a 32–0 record.
